reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive defect of pyrimidine biosynthesis caused by deficiency of uridine monophosphate synthase (UMPS)
Classically presents in infancy with a megaloblastic anaemia that does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate
Additional features include failure to thrive, developmental delay, and increased susceptibility to infection from immune impairment
The biochemical hallmark is greatly increased urinary orotic acid, which may crystallise and cause orotic acid crystalluria and obstructive uropathy
The impaired synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides limits DNA synthesis in the marrow, producing the megaloblastic picture despite normal haematinics
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating orotic aciduria with the typical anaemia, supported by enzyme assay and UMPS gene testing
Treatment is oral uridine replacement, which bypasses the enzyme block and typically corrects the anaemia and improves growth
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary orotic aciduria results from deficiency of uridine monophosphate synthase, the bifunctional enzyme that carries out the final two steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine monophosphate decarboxylase). The block prevents conversion of orotic acid to uridine monophosphate, so pyrimidine nucleotides required for nucleic acid synthesis are deficient while the upstream substrate orotic acid accumulates and is excreted in large amounts. The nucleotide shortage impairs rapidly dividing cells, most evident as megaloblastic anaemia and growth failure, and excess orotic acid can precipitate in the urinary tract. Because uridine is downstream of the block, its provision restores nucleotide supply.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemias
Secondary orotic aciduria from urea cycle disorders (e.g. OTC deficiency)
Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
Nutritional or malabsorptive causes of failure to thrive
Lysinuric protein intolerance with orotic aciduria
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing megaloblastic changes
Serum vitamin B12 and folate to exclude nutritional megaloblastosis
Plasma ammonia and amino acids to distinguish urea cycle causes of orotic aciduria
Molecular genetic testing of the UMPS gene
redFlags: Severe anaemia unresponsive to standard haematinics in an infant
Orotic acid crystalluria causing urinary obstruction
Significant developmental delay or failure to thrive
Recurrent or severe infections suggesting immune compromise
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and lifelong uridine replacement the haematological and growth abnormalities usually resolve and children can develop normally; untreated disease leads to persistent anaemia, growth failure and developmental impairment.
pitfalls: Assuming a megaloblastic anaemia must be due to B12 or folate deficiency and missing the diagnosis
Confusing primary orotic aciduria with the secondary orotic aciduria of urea cycle disorders
Overlooking orotic acid crystalluria as a cause of urinary obstruction
Discontinuing uridine, as the disorder requires lifelong replacement
Not offering genetic counselling for this recessive condition
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Start lifelong oral uridine replacement (uridine triacetate) to bypass the uridine monophosphate synthase block and restore pyrimidine nucleotide supply, correcting the megaloblastic anaemia and growth failure
Recognise that the anaemia does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, so these should not be relied upon as treatment
Maintain adequate hydration to reduce orotic acid crystalluria and the risk of obstructive uropathy
Monitor the full blood count, growth and development to titrate uridine therapy, and manage any urinary tract obstruction from orotic acid crystals
Coordinate care across metabolic medicine, paediatrics and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive UMPS inheritance with testing of at-risk family members
